status_reasoning: Reviewers note that Asakawa et al. (2005) previously demonstrated meiosis-specific outer kinetochore disassembly in S. pombe and its requirement for reductional segregation. They state the current study 'is an advance in important ways' but 'does not supersede' prior work, and that 'certain novelty claims are unwarranted and need rewriting.' The physiological role of outer kinetochore disassembly remains incompletely proven.

Reviewers express concern about the lack of comprehensive western blot data for CLB overexpression at the beginning of Results, noting 'it is important to see timing and know how the overexpression compares to the levels that normally form in WT.' They question whether phenotypic differences are due to 'kinase protein levels or activities' and whether Clb4's limited effects reflect 'specificity or levels,' indicating uncertainty about the interpretation of cyclin-specific effects.

Reviewers directly challenge the recombination data, stating 'FigureS1E shows that recombination is not normal in GAL-CLB3 cells - the crossovers form earlier (at least 1 hr and with biphasic kinetics) and at lower levels than seen in wild type.' They note 'the authors claim that recombination is normal when CLB3 is prematurely expressed. This is a contradiction that needs to be addressed' and question the accuracy of the quantification.

Reviewers express concern about 'the physiological relevance of a number of experiments,' asking 'how relevant is the pathology associated with very early, very high expression of Clb3 for understanding wild-type meiosis?' They note 'some conclusions remain speculative with the approach and should be stated as such' and that 'the introduction section does not make a link to how over-expression might be used to learn about the normal process.'

Reviewers note that 'artificial assembly of the outer kinetochore in prophase I (CUP-NDC80 CUP-HSK3) does not influence MI segregation unless CLB3 is also artificially expressed. This is an important paradox that must be addressed.' They state 'it remains completely unproven whether the physiological role of outer kinetochore disassembly in prophase I is to prevent premature spindle-kinetochore connections' and suggest alternative explanations for its function.

Reviewers raise timing concerns, noting 'CUP-CLB3 is induced so early that cells may still be in S phase' and 'the induction of Ndt80 expression at 4.5 hrs is also questionably early.' They request 'FACs analysis for representative time courses' and note 'there isn't a single time-course in this paper to demonstrate when MI occurs in a typical wild-type culture,' expressing uncertainty about the developmental timing of the experiments.

Reviewers state 'it is an overstatement to write categorically that the work shows two independent mechanisms for timely engagement of the microtubules with the kinetochore.' They suggest that 'manipulating the synthesis of the outer kinetochore proteins enhances the Cdk effects, but perhaps this is because the unknown kinase targets are not completely modified' and propose alternative interpretations involving transcriptional/translational regulation by CDK.

Reviewers acknowledge that the study shows 'this is due to early development of bipolar spindles' and that 'premature kinetochore-microtubule attachments disrupt normal morphogenesis of kinetochores and pericentric cohesion.' They describe the data as 'for the most part impeccable' and note 'cleverly designed and well-executed experiments,' indicating acceptance of the core experimental findings on cyclin-induced spindle formation and sister chromatid segregation.

Reviewers recognize the findings on monopolin localization defects as part of the 'several novel observations' and do not raise specific concerns about these data. The demonstration that premature microtubule-kinetochore interactions disrupt monopolin localization is implicitly accepted as part of the 'important and new discovery' regarding kinetochore morphogenesis.

Reviewers acknowledge that 'premature kinetochore-microtubule attachments disrupt normal morphogenesis of kinetochores and pericentric cohesion' and that 'a protective cohesin domain formed around the centromeres is an important and new discovery.' They describe this as part of the study's core contribution, with data that are 'for the most part impeccable,' indicating acceptance of the centromeric cohesin protection findings.

Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the ribosome profiling data or the correlation between Ndc80 protein levels and CLB3-induced phenotypes. These findings are part of the 'several novel observations' acknowledged by reviewers, and the data quality is described as 'for the most part impeccable.'

The experiments showing that coexpression of NDC80, HSK3, and CLB3 enhances sister chromatid segregation are not specifically criticized by reviewers. These data support the outer kinetochore regulation mechanism and are part of the 'cleverly designed and well-executed experiments' noted by reviewers.
